Senses.PreferredTarget: Reveal a jeweled Buddha land on the tip of a hair
SearchAliases: reveal a jeweled buddha land on the tip of a hair
Senses.Note: A jeweled Buddha land appears at a hair’s tip, often paired with turning a great teaching wheel in a speck of dust. Gulin says this reaches from a light already present in each person. Miyun uses it while directing an assembly toward a donor’s resting place; Feiyin includes it in a summer gathering that shares one field. Wanru places it after breaking ordinary time and scale. Shiyu asks why anyone would expend great effort on the display, while Yinyuan calls it a result of immediate recognition. The tiny point makes vastness a question for the present encounter.

Senses.Explanation: The jeweled Buddha land appearing on one hair tip brings the vast within the immediately small. Gulin, Miyun, and Feiyin use the image in different sermons about present light, a donor’s resting place, and summer dwelling. Wanru and Yinyuan relate it to immediate recognition; Shiyu asks why one would labor to exhibit it.

Senses.Explanation: A Buddha land appears on a hair tip; the great wheel of teaching turns in a speck of dust joins two images of vast activity in a minute place. Feiyin invokes the pair in a discussion of vastness in smallness, then says even this remains within a measurable realm. Yinyuan uses the same image at a festival and calls it part of teaching activity, short of the further turn. Ying’an places it in a hall address on a power that moves without leaving the present scene. Qianyan challenges a carver to show a Buddha body that cannot be measured by the statue alone. Lianfeng places the pair among the work of two temples and then refuses a simple claim that they are either different or identical. Yuansou applies it to the one who has broken through limiting names and can act freely in every place.

Fengxue Yanzhao contrasts establishing one mote, when the country flourishes but the old villager frowns, with establishing none, when the country perishes but the villager rests. If this is understood, he says, the listener has no share and all is the old monk; if it is not understood, the old monk is the listener. He then says the two can enlighten or mislead everyone and marks their positions by patting left and right. Xueyan Zuqin raises this address, adds Yunmen's easy-here/difficult-there reply and demands recognition of both elders. The headword is Fengxue's quoted conditional reversal, not a separate claim by the commentator that every person's identity has vanished.

Tianyin Yuanxiu quotes Fenyang's chrysanthemum address and its use of Fengxue's conditions, but interrupts the inherited speech with his own comments. To the no-share condition he allows granting and taking while warning against oppressing someone; to the old-monk-as-listener condition he allows killing and enlivening while warning against bringing about one's own collapse. He continues through the four host-and-guest relations and ends by raising his staff. Senses.Note: The pair belongs to Fashou Bodhisattva's answer in a scriptural verse. The longer verse compares hearing without action to a person swept by water who still dies of thirst and to a healer unable to cure his own illness. Tianran quotes the longer answer and applies it to his assembly. Senses.Note: The Complete Awakening teaching says to refrain from raising deluded thoughts and also from trying to extinguish them. Guantao asks what remains when bodily elements disperse; Pufu replies to the quoted passage with an everyday saying. Wansong turns it against a student’s claim to be free of sensory appearances. Beijian gives it a boat verse, and Zide asks what following it would look like. Each use resists making mental stillness into a thing to possess.

Senses.Explanation: The doubled cry of the Chan records: blue sky, blue sky — the exclamation of last resort when dismay, wonder, or the refusal to explain takes the voice. Zhaozhou Congshen answers a newcomer's plea for direction with the doubled cry alone, Pu'an Yinsu opens his own praise-verse with it — awakened to the birthless, talking without speaking of Chan, the two opened skin-flaps sweeping earth and heaven — Hanyue Fazang laments the painted-eye lacquer buckets racing from Tiantai and Nanyue to Hebei and Jiangnan, the mess not stopping in the eastern lands and the tangle beginning in the western heavens, and Tianyin Yuanxiu echoes his questioner's cry straight back, then verses that heaven has no cover and earth no bearer, the ten thousand images nowhere absent, the east village drinking and the west village dancing with no one to name as ruler. Muchen Daomin grants the failing monk his thirty blows to carry out and answers the plea to name where he went wrong with the doubled cry alone, Liangting Jingting finds the five-colored life-threads of the river festival a bewilderment with the cry itself added grief, Zishui wheels his whisk into nine circle-marks before any ancient buddha's birth and dares the hall to see — blue sky, blue sky — and Jifei Ruyi, praising the seventeenth ancestor who waited half a year with half his nostril gone and flew the father's shame abroad at a high price, rules that whether for the sparse or the dense it comes back to the same cry.

Senses.Explanation: “An undershirt clinging to the skin” is a fixed image for an intimate encumbrance that still has to fall away. In Yuanwu Keqin's Essentials, Xuefeng Yicun says that under Deshan's blow he seemed to shed a thousand layers of such skin-clinging shirts; the garment image measures release from what had remained painfully close.
